extracted.intended_audience: UIC administrators, Agents II, Benefit Control Officers (BCOs), chairmen/members of Boards of referees and Umpires, and policymakers drafting/regulating unemployment insurance adjudicative procedure
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural recommendations for fact-finding, documentation, hearings, and claimant participation in unemployment insurance adjudication and appeals (procedures for Agents II, BCOs, Boards of referees, the Umpire, and the UIC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of third-party informant sources when crucial and contradicted
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases where the information obtained is a crucial factor in the decision and is contradicted by the claimant, the UIC should not refuse to divulge the source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although sec.115 grants immunity to informants and UIC practice normally withholds sources before litigation, when third-party information is decisive and contested the source must be disclosed so the claimant can contest it. Note tension between protecting informants and ensuring fairness to claimants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chairman's introductory statement at Board hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: The chairman of the Board of referees should open every hearing with a brief statement introducing the members, mentioning their respective status, reminding the claimant they represent the two classes of contributors and are independent of the UIC, explaining the purpose of the hearing and stressing the informal and confidential nature of the proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UIC should issue a circular letter reminding chairmen of this obligation and provide a standard format listing points to be covered (including presence of clerk and tape recording). Current practice varies; some chairmen merely introduce members. Standardization improves claimant reassurance and hearing atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-maker must have sufficient information via oral or written investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The author of an administrative decision should have available sufficient information on the circumstances of the case, acquired either by inquiring directly of those involved (oral investigation) or on the basis of written documents (written investigation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before applying law to facts, the decision-maker must weight items of information according to criteria (often derived from law but extraneous to it). The chapter separates gathering facts, documentation available, and assessment of facts as distinct tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid leading questions in BCO interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Leading or suggestive questions asked by BCOs should be used sparingly, and answers to them should be checked by other, more direct questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggestiveness varies with subject, tone and claimant. Some leading questions are fair, but they risk distorting facts. Use follow-up direct questioning to verify responses. This is part of protecting accuracy of interview reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit third parties at benefit-control interviews to reduce traps
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitting third parties to be present at benefit-control interviews reduces the risk that BCOs can 'lay traps' for interviewees and helps claimants with insufficient knowledge of official languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize this as an effort to deal openly with claimants; it should reduce misunderstanding, distortion and intimidation. Expect it to make it harder for BCOs to use suggestive tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect claimants from coerced signing; allow dispute of interview report before decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Where reports of interviews are read to (rather than signed by) the claimant, this protects against allegations of being pressured into signing; more importantly, the claimant must have an opportunity to dispute the accuracy of the report before a decision is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading the report to the claimant is preferable to requiring signature, but does not eliminate all inaccuracies. The crucial procedural right is the chance to dispute/report corrections before the decision—ensure this opportunity is provided (see cross-reference to later chapter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify guidelines on penalties and structure Agent II discretion regarding 'fraudulous intent'
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines concerning penalties should be clearer about the range of mitigating circumstances and provide a clearer structure for the exercise of an Agent II's discretion in determining the presence of 'fraudulous intent'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents II and BCOs already take circumstances into account when choosing between administrative penalties and prosecution; the Guidelines should explicitly enumerate mitigating factors and structure discretion (see cross-reference to Chapter 14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal tribunals should grant hearings and actively summon appellants/witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: The appeal bodies are required to grant a hearing to anyone who requests one and are authorized to summon the appellant or any person whose testimony has a bearing on the case; these powers are insufficiently used and should be employed more often.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many appeals are decided on submissions alone (appellant absent), which correlates with lower success rates, chairmen of Boards of referees and Agents II should more extensively use their power to summon appellants and useful witnesses. Failure to summon introduces uncertainty and error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid formal adversarial representation by UIC at Board hearings (limit UIC participation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although UIC participation is not prohibited, development of a symmetrical adversary system at Board hearings would formalize proceedings, introducing cross-examination and pleadings, which would undermine the relaxed, informal and quick fact-finding valued in Boards of referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UIC should generally refrain from being represented before the Board except in more complex cases (e.g., labour disputes). The risk is increasing UIC resource superiority and loss of informal advantages; formalization trend should be arrested rather than encouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardize submission (summary of the file) content and format
rubrics_metrics.description: The submission to the Board of referees (better called a 'summary of the file') should always include: (1) basic information about the claim; (2) a type-written complete transcript of all items placed in the file since initial application, particularly correspondence and telephone notes; (3) an indication of relevant facts not provided by those documents, e.g., medical yardsticks and labour market statistics; (4) a statement of factual and legal reasons cited by the Agent II in support of his decision; and (5) a summary of applicable caselaw with quotations of the most significant passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are current discrepancies between regions/districts in format/content; an internal UIC directive should standardize this. Agents II should be assisted by Insurance Advisory Services in researching caselaw. Expanding the scope makes 'summary of the file' a more accurate name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require statutory deadlines and delivery rules for submission summaries with sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The summary of the file should be written and communicated to the appellant and interested third parties within fourteen days of receipt of the appeal (with possible 14-day extension by notice), and members of the Board should receive it at least seven days before the hearing; failure to produce a summary within the prescribed period should result in the appeal being deemed allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transposing reg.180 into the Act would make preparation/communication mandatory; including deadlines prevents the argument that Board members need not read the summary before the hearing and gives the chairman time to decide whom to summon. Claimants retain the right to request corrections before the hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation on employers to provide Record of Employment and penalties for delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers should be required by the Act (not merely Regulations) to issue Records of Employment within a prescribed period (proposal: extend from five to ten days), and forceful steps (prosecutions or administrative penalties) should be taken against negligent employers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transposing reg.146 into the Act gives the obligation more formality and increases courts' willingness to penalize. Proposed penalty: for each week of delay, an employer could be fined an amount equal to the claimant's weekly benefit, imposed by Agent II with District Manager approval; employer can avoid penalty by showing due diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tape-record all hearings before Boards of referees and retain recordings until appeal expiry
rubrics_metrics.description: All appeals which result in a hearing should be tape-recorded; recordings could be kept by the UIC until after expiry of the right of appeal and transcribed only if the case is appealed to the second level of review (the Umpire).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Currently only labour-dispute hearings are routinely taped; expanding this practice is simple and relatively inexpensive and would be extremely useful to the Umpire on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prescribe and publish the formula/factors for determining the 'reasonable interval'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act should indicate precisely the basis for determining what constitutes a 'reasonable interval' (the period after which a claimant must accept suitable employment), and the details of the formula should be embodied in the Regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed new subsection (4) lists factors: (a) nature of claimant's usual occupation; (b) the market for employment in claimant's region; (c) length of time the claimant has worked in his usual occupation; (d) how much time has elapsed since interruption of earnings. Publishing the logic improves claimant awareness and reduces arbitrariness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose medical yardsticks used in decisions and allow claimant rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.description: When information derived from the UIC's medical yardsticks was a factor in a decision on sickness benefit, the UIC should reveal that information at the time it notifies the claimant and the claimant should then have an opportunity to provide contrary scientific evidence (own doctor or UIC-approved physicians).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medical yardsticks are internal documents; Boards of referees should regard yardsticks-derived information as one piece of evidence to be weighed like any other. It is unacceptable to apply an extra-legal criterion to an individual without informing them and permitting rebuttal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use labour market statistics cautiously and only with comparable supply/demand data
rubrics_metrics.description: Labour market statistics may be used to decide Active Job Search Program eligibility and to evaluate claimant efforts, but they are often unsatisfactory; Agents should use supply figures only if they have comparable demand statistics and generally treat such statistics only as a guide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistics are irregular, geographically mismatched and derived from incomplete sources (CMC listings, newspapers). Evaluation of claimant efforts (e.g., five applications) must account for demand-side context (e.g., number of applicants). Boards of referees usually rely on local knowledge, which is preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decentralize offices and establish small local units to improve access
rubrics_metrics.description: Decentralized, small administrative units (type 3A offices) with an office manager, receptionist, a service unit, a BCO and claimants' files are efficient and self-sufficient, enabling most administrative procedures to be concluded without involving another office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such offices require modest space, blend into the landscape and create an atmosphere more like an insurance agency than a bureaucratic factory; decentralization facilitates public participation and access to decision-makers.
